topics.name: September 11 attacks
topics.kicker: 2001 al-Qaeda attacks on the U.S. · Deadliest terrorist attack in history
topics.briefing: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four airliners. Two struck the Twin Towers of New York City’s World Trade Center, which both collapsed; one hit the Pentagon, near Washington, D.C.; and the fourth crashed in a Pennsylvania field after its passengers fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people, making them the deadliest terrorist attack in history. Two memorial pools, opened in 2011, mark where the towers stood.
topics.answerHtml: September 11 attacks (or 9/11; prompt on descriptions like an attack on the World Trade Center or the Twin Towers; do not accept “1993 World Trade Center bombing”)
prompt: attack on the world trade center
attacks on the world trade center

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The New York Philharmonic asked composer John Adams to write _On the Transmigration of Souls_ in memory of the people killed in this event. That piece premiered about a year after this event and won the 2003 Pulitzer Prize for Music.
tossups.r: In this event, hijacked planes destroyed the Twin Towers in New York City. For 10 points, name these 2001 terrorist attacks.

tossups.p: The musical _Come From Away_ tells how the small town of Gander, Newfoundland, welcomed thousands of stranded airline passengers whose flights were diverted to Canada during this event. That day, every civilian plane flying over the United States was ordered to land at the nearest airport.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attacks in which al-Qaeda hijackers crashed planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: A 2004 report on this event blamed a “failure of imagination” and recommended creating a Director of National Intelligence to oversee the nation’s intelligence agencies. Former New Jersey governor Thomas Kean chaired the commission that wrote that report, and Lee Hamilton was its vice chair.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 terrorist attacks that destroyed the Twin Towers in New York City.

tossups.p: An official report called Khalid Sheikh Mohammed the “principal architect” of this event; he was captured in Pakistan in 2003 and later held at the U.S. prison at Guantánamo [“gwahn-TAH-nuh-moh”] Bay, Cuba. His nephew, Ramzi Yousef, had planned a 1993 truck bombing of one of this event’s targets.
tossups.r: Mohamed Atta led the 19 hijackers in this event. For 10 points, name these al-Qaeda attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: During this event, President George W. Bush was listening to a class of second-graders read a story called “The Pet Goat” at Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida. His chief of staff, Andrew Card, leaned over and whispered that “America is under attack.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks in which hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center.

tossups.p: Three days after this event, President George W. Bush climbed onto a pile of rubble and answered rescue workers through a bullhorn: “I can hear you!” That year, _Time_ named New York mayor Rudy Giuliani its Person of the Year for leading the city’s response.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 terrorist attacks in which hijacked airliners struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: The Tower of Voices, a memorial near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, holds 40 wind chimes, one for each passenger and crew member killed when their plane crashed in a nearby field during this event. Those passengers had learned through phone calls about the other attacks and decided to fight back against the hijackers.
tossups.r: That plane was United Flight 93. For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks that also struck the Pentagon.

tossups.p: A Callery pear tree nicknamed the “Survivor Tree” was pulled from the wreckage after this event, nursed back to health, and replanted at a memorial designed by Michael Arad. That memorial, called _Reflecting Absence_, has two square pools that sit in the footprints of two destroyed skyscrapers.
tossups.r: Hijacked planes had struck those towers. For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: Bronze panels around a memorial’s pools list 2,983 names, including six people killed in a 1993 bombing at the same site. That memorial was dedicated on the tenth anniversary of this event, in 2011, and a museum beneath it opened three years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks, which killed 2,977 people in New York, Virginia, and Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: A memorial in Arlington, Virginia, opened in 2008 with 184 benches, one for each person killed at a nearby military headquarters during this event. Most of those victims worked inside that building, and the rest were aboard American Airlines Flight 77.
tossups.r: That building was the Pentagon. For 10 points, name these 2001 terrorist attacks, which also destroyed the World Trade Center.

tossups.p: Once nicknamed the “Freedom Tower,” a skyscraper built after this event rises exactly 1,776 feet to honor the year the Declaration of Independence was signed. When it opened in 2014, it was the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.
tossups.r: It stands at the rebuilt World Trade Center. For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks that destroyed the original Twin Towers.

tossups.p: For the first time in its history, NATO invoked Article 5, which says that an attack on one member is an attack on all, the day after this event. Less than a month later, the United States and its allies began a war to drive the Taliban from power in Afghanistan.
tossups.r: Osama bin Laden, the al-Qaeda leader behind this event, was killed in Pakistan in 2011. For 10 points, name these al-Qaeda attacks on the United States.

tossups.p: About six weeks after this event, President George W. Bush signed the USA PATRIOT Act, which expanded the government’s power to watch and investigate suspected terrorists. In 2002, Congress combined 22 agencies into a new Department of Homeland Security, first led by Tom Ridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: In Jonathan Safran Foer’s novel _Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close_, nine-year-old Oskar Schell searches New York City for the lock that fits a key left by his father, who died in this event. Paul Greengrass directed _United 93_, a 2006 film about one of the planes in this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks in which hijacked airliners hit the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

tossups.p: The New York City Fire Department lost 343 of its members in this event, including its chaplain, Father Mychal Judge, who was officially listed as the event’s first recorded victim. For months afterward, workers searched and cleared the site, which became known as Ground Zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 2001 attacks in which two hijacked planes destroyed the Twin Towers.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, called the plot’s “principal architect,” was captured in Pakistan in 2003 and later held at Guantánamo Bay

trap.title: 1993 or 2001?
trap.body: The World Trade Center was attacked twice. On February 26, 1993, a truck bomb exploded in a parking garage beneath the North Tower, killing six people; that bombing is a different answer line, even though its victims’ names are also on the memorial. Many questions also mention Osama bin Laden or al-Qaeda early, and a player who blurts out the man or the group instead of the event loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Hijacked airliners, the Pentagon, Flight 93, Shanksville, and 2,977 victims mean 2001; a truck bomb, an underground garage, and Ramzi Yousef mean 1993. Listen for the noun: “this event” or “these attacks” wants the attacks, “this man” wants Osama bin Laden, and “this group” wants al-Qaeda.
trap.line: Real answer line: September 11 attacks (or 9/11; do not accept “1993 World Trade Center bombing”)

topics.name: Aaron Burr
topics.kicker: 3rd U.S. Vice President · Killed Alexander Hamilton in an 1804 duel
topics.briefing: Aaron Burr tied Thomas Jefferson in the presidential election of 1800 and became the third vice president instead. In 1804, while still vice president, he shot and killed his longtime rival Alexander Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. Three years later he was tried for treason, accused of plotting to break off part of the West or invade Spanish Mexico, but he was found not guilty at a trial run by Chief Justice John Marshall.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The first “Got Milk?” TV commercial, aired in 1993, showed a history buff who could not win a radio quiz because a mouthful of peanut butter kept him from clearly saying this man’s name. This man sings “Wait for It” in a 2015 Broadway musical.
tossups.r: That musical is named for the Treasury secretary this man killed in a duel. For 10 points, name this third vice president.

tossups.p: This man founded the Manhattan Company, which was chartered to bring clean water to New York City but used a clause in its charter to open a bank that became part of JPMorgan Chase. In 1800, his organizing in New York City, with help from the Society of St. Tammany, won the state for his party.
tossups.r: The next year, he became Thomas Jefferson’s vice president. For 10 points, name this man who killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

tossups.p: This man’s grandfather was the preacher Jonathan Edwards, who gave the sermon “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,” and his father, who had the same name, was president of the College of New Jersey. This man graduated from that school, later renamed Princeton, at age 16.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who tied Thomas Jefferson in the election of 1800 and later killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

tossups.p: During the American Revolution, this young officer marched through the Maine wilderness with Benedict Arnold and served as an aide to General Richard Montgomery, who was killed in the failed attack on Quebec City. This officer later commanded troops at the Battle of Monmouth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later became Thomas Jefferson’s vice president and killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

tossups.p: In 1791, this man won a U.S. Senate seat from New York by defeating Philip Schuyler, the father-in-law of a rival lawyer. Six years later, this man helped settle a bitter quarrel between that rival and James Monroe.
tossups.r: That rival was Alexander Hamilton, whom this man later killed in a duel. For 10 points, name this third vice president.

tossups.p: James Bayard, Delaware’s only congressman, helped break a deadlock between this man and his running mate by casting a blank ballot on the House of Representatives’ 36th vote. To prevent another tie like that one, the states ratified the Twelfth Amendment.
tossups.r: That running mate, Thomas Jefferson, became president. For 10 points, name this man who became vice president instead and later killed Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: As president of the Senate, this man presided over the 1805 impeachment trial of Supreme Court Justice Samuel Chase, who was acquitted. Soon after, this man gave an emotional farewell speech calling the Senate a “citadel of law, of order, and of liberty.”
tossups.r: Days later, his term as Thomas Jefferson’s vice president ended. For 10 points, name this man, who had killed Alexander Hamilton the year before.

tossups.p: After losing the 1804 race for governor of New York to Morgan Lewis, this man read a newspaper letter by Dr. Charles Cooper saying that a rival had expressed a “despicable opinion” of him. This man demanded an explanation, and their angry letters went back and forth for weeks.
tossups.r: The two men finally met at Weehawken, New Jersey, where this man fatally shot Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this vice president.

tossups.p: Some New England Federalists hoped this man would lead New York into a breakaway northern confederacy if he won the 1804 race for governor. Later that year, he was charged with crimes in both New York and New Jersey, including murder, but he never stood trial.
tossups.r: Those charges came after he shot Alexander Hamilton in a duel. For 10 points, name this vice president under Thomas Jefferson.

tossups.p: This man gathered men and boats on Harman Blennerhassett’s [“BLEN-er-HASS-it”] island in the Ohio River, and he exchanged coded letters with General James Wilkinson, who was secretly taking money from Spain. Wilkinson betrayed him by sending one of those letters to President Thomas Jefferson.
tossups.r: This man was then arrested and tried for treason. For 10 points, name this former vice president who had killed Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: At this man’s 1807 trial in Richmond, the judge ordered President Thomas Jefferson to turn over a letter, a ruling later cited in arguments about executive privilege. That judge then ruled that treason required two witnesses to an actual act of war, and this man was found not guilty.
tossups.r: That judge was Chief Justice John Marshall. For 10 points, name this former vice president, who had killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

tossups.p: This man gave his daughter Theodosia [“thee-uh-DOH-shuh”] an unusually strong education, and he was heartbroken when her ship vanished off the Carolina coast in 1813. Her husband, Joseph Alston, was governor of South Carolina at the time.
tossups.r: In the musical _Hamilton_, this man sings “Dear Theodosia” to her. For 10 points, name this vice president who killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

tossups.p: In 1833, this man married the wealthy widow Eliza Jumel in her Manhattan mansion, which had served as George Washington’s headquarters in 1776. She soon filed for divorce, and it was granted on the day he died in 1836.
tossups.r: Her lawyer was Alexander Hamilton Jr., a son of the man this man had killed in a duel. For 10 points, name this third vice president.

tossups.p: Gore Vidal wrote a 1973 historical novel named for this man, who was one of New York’s best-known lawyers. Leslie Odom Jr. won a Tony Award for playing this man in a 2015 musical, where he complains that he was not in “The Room Where It Happens.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this third vice president, who killed Alexander Hamilton in an 1804 duel.

tossups.p: In 1807, this man was arrested in what is now Alabama while trying to escape to Spanish Florida, after President Thomas Jefferson had told Congress that his guilt was “beyond question.” After his trial, he spent four years in Europe, seeking support for his schemes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vice president who was tried for treason three years after he killed Alexander Hamilton.

clues.t: Killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804
Third vice president of the United States (1801–1805), under Thomas Jefferson
Tied his running mate, Thomas Jefferson, with 73 electoral votes each in the election of 1800
Tried for treason in 1807 and found not guilty
Narrator and rival in the 2015 musical _Hamilton_; sings “Wait for It” and “The Room Where It Happens”
The House of Representatives broke the 1800 tie on its 36th ballot; the Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, was adopted to prevent such ties
Chief Justice John Marshall ran his trial in Richmond and ruled that treason needs two witnesses to an actual act of war
Accused of plotting to break western lands away from the U.S. or to invade Spanish Mexico, a scheme called his “conspiracy”
General James Wilkinson, his partner and secretly a paid Spanish agent, betrayed him to President Jefferson
Gathered men and boats on Harman Blennerhassett’s island in the Ohio River (1806)
Challenged Hamilton after Dr. Charles Cooper’s letter reported Hamilton’s “despicable opinion” of him
Lost the 1804 race for governor of New York to Morgan Lewis while still vice president
U.S. senator from New York (1791–1797); won the seat by defeating Hamilton’s father-in-law, Philip Schuyler
His trial judge ordered President Jefferson to turn over documents, a ruling later cited in executive privilege cases
The first “Got Milk?” commercial (1993): a mouthful of peanut butter keeps a history buff from saying his name in a radio contest
Founded the Manhattan Company (1799), a water company that opened a bank; it became part of JPMorgan Chase, which owns the duel pistols
Used the Society of St. Tammany to help win New York City, and the state, for the Democratic-Republicans in 1800
Grandson of preacher Jonathan Edwards; his father of the same name was president of the College of New Jersey (Princeton)
Marched with Benedict Arnold and was an aide to Richard Montgomery in the failed attack on Quebec (1775)
James Bayard, Delaware’s only congressman, helped end the 1801 House deadlock with a blank ballot
Presided over the Senate impeachment trial of Justice Samuel Chase (1805); his farewell speech called the Senate a “citadel of law”
Charged with crimes, including murder, in New York and New Jersey after the duel, but never tried
Some New England Federalists, such as Timothy Pickering, hoped he would lead New York into a northern confederacy (1804)
Arrested in 1807 in present-day Alabama while fleeing toward Spanish Florida; Jefferson had told Congress his guilt was “beyond question”
His daughter Theodosia was lost at sea in 1813; her husband, Joseph Alston, was governor of South Carolina
Married wealthy widow Eliza Jumel (1833); the divorce was granted the day he died (1836), and her lawyer was Alexander Hamilton Jr.
After his trial, spent four years in Europe (1808–1812) seeking support for his schemes
Subject of Gore Vidal’s 1973 novel; Leslie Odom Jr. won a Tony Award for playing him

trap.title: Shooter or victim?
trap.body: The 1804 duel at Weehawken is a stock clue for both Aaron Burr and Alexander Hamilton, so a player who buzzes on “duel” without hearing who died can lose the tossup. Clues like Philip Schuyler and the 1804 New York governor’s race show up in both men’s questions, and the tied election of 1800 is also a stock clue for Thomas Jefferson.
trap.fix: Burr fired the fatal shot: he was Jefferson’s vice president and was later tried for treason. Hamilton was the one killed: the first Treasury secretary, the face on the $10 bill, and the main author of _The Federalist Papers_. If a question asks for “this event,” say “the Burr–Hamilton duel.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Aaron Burr (do not accept “Alexander Hamilton”)

topics.name: American Civil War
topics.kicker: Union vs. Confederacy, 1861–1865 · Deadliest war in U.S. history
topics.briefing: After Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860, eleven Southern states eventually broke away to protect slavery and formed the Confederate States of America. The war began in April 1861, when Confederates fired on Fort Sumter, and it raged for four years, from Bull Run to Gettysburg to Appomattox, where Robert E. Lee surrendered in 1865. An estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers died, and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery.
topics.answerHtml: American Civil War (or War Between the States; or War of the Rebellion; or War of Secession; do not accept other civil wars, such as the “English Civil War”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Wilmer McLean is said to have joked that this war “began in my front yard and ended in my front parlor.” His farm near Manassas was caught up in the war’s first major battle, and he then moved to a Virginia village where the war’s best-known surrender later took place in his home.
tossups.r: There, Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1861 to 1865.

tossups.p: Captain Charles Wilkes of the USS _San Jacinto_ stopped the British mail ship _Trent_ and seized two diplomats, James Mason and John Slidell, during this war. To avoid a second war, this time with Britain, the U.S. government soon set the two men free.
tossups.r: Mason and Slidell had been sent to Europe by the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this war in which Abraham Lincoln led the Union.

tossups.p: Before this war began, Senator John Crittenden of Kentucky proposed constitutional amendments to protect slavery south of the old Missouri Compromise line, but his plan failed. Weeks before the fighting started, Alexander Stephens declared in his “Cornerstone Speech” that his new government rested on slavery.
tossups.r: Stephens was vice president of the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this war that began in 1861 when Confederates fired on Fort Sumter.

tossups.p: During this war, one side passed the first national draft law in American history, and a later law excused one white man from service on any plantation with twenty or more enslaved people. The other side’s draft let a man pay $300 to avoid serving, which helped spark deadly riots in New York City in 1863.
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln led the Union in this war. For 10 points, name this war that began when Confederates fired on Fort Sumter.

tossups.p: Ken Burns’s 1990 PBS documentary series about this war used Jay Ungar’s fiddle tune “Ashokan Farewell” as its theme and made the historian Shelby Foote famous. Burns told the story largely through old photographs, many of them taken by Mathew Brady and his team.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Ulysses S. Grant defeated Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: In 1864, during this war, the _H. L. Hunley_ became the first submarine to sink an enemy warship when it sank the USS _Housatonic_ near Charleston. Two years earlier, the ironclads USS _Monitor_ and CSS _Virginia_ had fought the first battle between ironclad warships, at Hampton Roads.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war fought between the Union and the Confederacy from 1861 to 1865.

tossups.p: During this war, Harriet Tubman helped guide the Combahee [“KUM-bee”] River Raid, which freed more than 700 enslaved people in South Carolina. Weeks later, the 54th Massachusetts, a Black regiment led by Robert Gould Shaw, attacked Fort Wagner, as shown in the film _Glory_.
tossups.r: About 180,000 Black soldiers served in the Union Army in this war. For 10 points, name this war that began at Fort Sumter in 1861.

tossups.p: Dorothea Dix was put in charge of the U.S. Army’s nurses during this war, and Mary Edwards Walker became the only woman ever awarded the Medal of Honor, for her work as a surgeon in it. About two of every three soldiers who died in this war died of disease.
tossups.r: Clara Barton was called the “Angel of the Battlefield” in this war. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1861 to 1865.

tossups.p: Henry Fleming runs away from his first battle in this war but later carries his regiment’s flag in Stephen Crane’s novel _The Red Badge of Courage_. Julia Ward Howe wrote “The Battle Hymn of the Republic” early in this war, setting it to the tune of “John Brown’s Body.”
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln was president during this war. For 10 points, name this war that began with the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter.

tossups.p: Former Ohio congressman Clement Vallandigham [“vuh-LAN-dih-gum”], a leader of the antiwar Democrats called Copperheads, was arrested and sent across enemy lines during this war. After it ended, the Supreme Court ruled in _Ex parte Milligan_ that civilians could not be tried by military courts where regular courts were open.
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln also suspended habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”] during this war. For 10 points, name this war in which he led the Union against the Confederacy.

tossups.p: The warship CSS _Shenandoah_ did not surrender until November 1865, in Liverpool, England, months after the major armies in this war had stopped fighting. On June 19, 1865, General Gordon Granger announced in Galveston that the enslaved people of Texas were free.
tossups.r: That day is celebrated as Juneteenth. For 10 points, name this war that ended after Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House.

tossups.p: In this war, Union armies usually named battles after nearby streams, while their enemies named them after nearby towns, so the first major battle is called both Bull Run and Manassas. In that battle, Thomas Jackson earned the nickname “Stonewall.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederacy’s Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: Leaders of one side in this war believed that “King Cotton” would force Britain and France to help them, and they even held back cotton shipments in 1861 to prove it. The Battle of Antietam discouraged both countries from recognizing their government, and neither ever did.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war between the United States and the Confederate States of America, which ended in 1865.

tossups.p: To pay for this war, Congress passed the first federal income tax and the Legal Tender Act, which created paper money nicknamed “greenbacks.” With Southern lawmakers gone, Congress also passed the Homestead Act and the Morrill Act, which gave land to the states to start colleges.
tossups.r: All of those laws were signed by Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this war during which Lincoln also issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

tossups.p: During this war, the western counties of Virginia broke away to form West Virginia, which became a state in 1863. Four slave states, Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, and Delaware, stayed loyal to the national government and were called “border states.”
tossups.r: Late in this war, William Tecumseh Sherman marched from Atlanta to the sea. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1865.

clues.t: Fought from 1861 to 1865 between the Union (the North) and the Confederate States of America (the South)
Began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate cannons fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina
Abraham Lincoln led the Union; Jefferson Davis was president of the Confederacy
Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865
Eleven Southern states seceded, mainly to protect slavery, after Lincoln won the election of 1860
The deadliest war in U.S. history: an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers died, about two-thirds of them from disease
Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation took effect January 1, 1863; the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) ended slavery
Turning point, July 1863: the Union won at Gettysburg and captured Vicksburg, Mississippi
First major battle: First Bull Run (Manassas), July 1861, where Thomas Jackson earned the nickname “Stonewall”
Antietam (September 17, 1862) was the bloodiest single day in American history
The Union’s Anaconda Plan: blockade Southern ports and take control of the Mississippi River
William Tecumseh Sherman captured Atlanta (1864) and marched to the sea at Savannah, waging “total war”
First battle between ironclad warships: USS _Monitor_ vs. CSS _Virginia_ (the rebuilt _Merrimack_) at Hampton Roads (1862)
About 180,000 Black soldiers served in the Union Army, including the 54th Massachusetts, which attacked Fort Wagner (the film _Glory_)
Four slave “border states” stayed in the Union: Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, and Delaware; West Virginia split from Virginia (1863)
Wilmer McLean’s farm was caught up in First Bull Run, and Lee later surrendered in his parlor; he supposedly joked the war “began in my front yard…”
Trent Affair (1861): Charles Wilkes seized Confederate envoys James Mason and John Slidell from a British ship; they were released
Alexander Stephens’s “Cornerstone Speech” (March 1861) said the Confederacy rested on slavery; the Crittenden Compromise had failed
The Confederate draft (1862) was the first in American history; the Union’s $300 exemption helped spark the New York City draft riots (1863)
Ken Burns’s 1990 PBS documentary series; its theme was Jay Ungar’s “Ashokan Farewell,” and historian Shelby Foote became famous
The _H. L. Hunley_ became the first submarine to sink an enemy warship, the USS _Housatonic_ (1864)
Harriet Tubman helped guide the Combahee River Raid (1863), which freed more than 700 enslaved people
Clara Barton (“Angel of the Battlefield”), nurse chief Dorothea Dix, and surgeon Mary Edwards Walker, the only woman awarded the Medal of Honor
Stephen Crane’s _The Red Badge of Courage_ (Henry Fleming) and Julia Ward Howe’s “The Battle Hymn of the Republic”
Copperheads were antiwar Northern Democrats; Clement Vallandigham was banished to the South; _Ex parte Milligan_ (1866) limited military trials
“King Cotton” diplomacy failed: Britain and France never recognized the Confederacy
Wartime laws: the first federal income tax, paper “greenbacks” (Legal Tender Act), and the Homestead and Morrill Acts (1862)
Juneteenth: on June 19, 1865, General Gordon Granger announced freedom in Galveston, Texas; the CSS _Shenandoah_ surrendered last (November 1865)

trap.title: Part or whole war?
trap.body: Many of this war’s stock clues are also answer lines of their own: Fort Sumter, the Battle of Gettysburg, the Emancipation Proclamation, the Anaconda Plan, and Reconstruction, the era that came after it. Naming one of those when the question wants the whole war loses the tossup, and so does naming the whole war when the question wants the battle or the plan. In world history, saying only “Civil War” is not enough for the English or Spanish Civil War.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this war” or “this conflict” wants the American Civil War, while “this battle,” “this fort,” “this plan,” “this document,” or “this era” wants something more specific. If the question is about Oliver Cromwell or Francisco Franco, add “English” or “Spanish.”
trap.line: Real answer line: American Civil War (or War Between the States; or War of the Rebellion; or War of Secession; do not accept other civil wars, such as the “English Civil War”)

topics.name: Anaconda Plan
topics.kicker: Winfield Scott’s 1861 Union strategy · Blockade the coast, seize the Mississippi
topics.briefing: In 1861, the 74-year-old Union general Winfield Scott proposed a slow squeeze: blockade the Confederacy’s coastline and send gunboats and troops down the Mississippi River to split the South in two. Impatient Northerners wanted a quick march on Richmond instead, and critics mocked his idea by naming it after a giant snake that squeezes its prey. The war took four years, and the Union ended up doing much of what Scott had planned.
topics.answerHtml: Anaconda Plan (prompt on the Union blockade of the South, Scott’s plan, or Scott’s Great Snake)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After two victories completed this plan’s goal on one river, Abraham Lincoln wrote in a letter to James Conkling that “the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea.” Those victories were the captures of Vicksburg, Mississippi, and Port Hudson, Louisiana, in July 1863.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan by Winfield Scott to blockade the South and seize the Mississippi River, named for a snake.

tossups.p: In the 1863 _Prize Cases_, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that the president could order one part of this plan without a declaration of war from Congress. Abraham Lincoln had proclaimed that part on April 19, 1861, a week after the attack on Fort Sumter.
tossups.r: That part was a naval blockade of Southern ports. For 10 points, name this Union strategy proposed by Winfield Scott.

tossups.p: The capture of Fort Fisher in January 1865 closed Wilmington, North Carolina, the most important port the Confederacy had left for ships slipping past one part of this plan. Those low, fast steamers often carried cotton out to Nassau or Bermuda and brought weapons back.
tossups.r: Those ships were called blockade runners. For 10 points, name this Union strategy of Winfield Scott, named for a snake that squeezes its prey.

tossups.p: In Margaret Mitchell’s novel _Gone with the Wind_, Rhett Butler makes a fortune by sneaking ships past one part of this plan. Many real ships that did the same thing sailed from Nassau in the Bahamas.
tossups.r: That part of this plan was a naval blockade of Southern ports. For 10 points, name this strategy proposed by Winfield Scott in 1861.

tossups.p: Northern newspapers led by Horace Greeley’s _New-York Tribune_ rejected this slow plan and demanded a quick march on Richmond. That pressure helped push the Union army into the First Battle of Bull Run, where it suffered a stunning defeat in July 1861.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan by General Winfield Scott to squeeze the South with a blockade and control of the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: In letters to George McClellan in May 1861, this plan’s author predicted that it would bring the South to terms with less bloodshed than any other strategy. That author, then 74 years old, was too old and ill to lead an army in the field.
tossups.r: That author was Winfield Scott, nicknamed “Old Fuss and Feathers.” For 10 points, name this plan to blockade the South and control the Mississippi.

tossups.p: In August 1864, David Farragut led a fleet past underwater mines, then called “torpedoes,” to close Mobile Bay, Alabama, one of the last Gulf ports used by ships slipping past one part of this plan. Two years earlier, Farragut had captured New Orleans.
tossups.r: An 1861 cartoon map called this plan “Scott’s Great Snake.” For 10 points, name this Union strategy to blockade the South and take the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: To carry out the river half of this plan, engineer James Eads built a fleet of ironclad gunboats, including the USS _Cairo_, which a mine sank in the Yazoo River in December 1862. The _Cairo_ was raised a century later and put on display at Vicksburg.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union strategy, proposed by Winfield Scott, to control the Mississippi River and blockade the South.

tossups.p: In April 1862, John Pope’s army and Andrew Foote’s gunboats captured the Confederate defenses on Island No. 10, opening more of one river for this plan. Weeks later, David Farragut’s fleet ran past Forts Jackson and St. Philip and captured New Orleans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union strategy to take control of the Mississippi River and blockade the Confederacy, named for a giant snake.

tossups.p: Nathaniel Banks’s army besieged Port Hudson, Louisiana, for about seven weeks, and its surrender in July 1863 completed one goal of this plan. Five days earlier, John C. Pemberton had surrendered Vicksburg to Ulysses S. Grant.
tossups.r: Those victories split the Confederacy in two. For 10 points, name this plan by Winfield Scott to control the Mississippi River and blockade Southern ports.

tossups.p: In November 1861, a fleet under Samuel Du Pont captured Port Royal Sound in South Carolina so that ships enforcing one part of this plan would have a base for coal and supplies. Navy Secretary Gideon Welles divided those ships into squadrons along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union strategy to blockade the Confederacy and seize the Mississippi River, named for a snake.

tossups.p: On March 8, 1862, the ironclad CSS _Virginia_ tried to break one part of this plan at Hampton Roads by sinking the USS _Cumberland_ and destroying the USS _Congress_. The next day, the newly arrived USS _Monitor_ fought the _Virginia_ to a draw.
tossups.r: That part of this plan was the Union’s naval blockade of the South. For 10 points, name this strategy proposed by Winfield Scott.

tossups.p: One goal of this plan was to cut off Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana west of the river from the rest of the Confederacy, along with the cattle and supplies those lands sent east. Ulysses S. Grant’s capture of Vicksburg in 1863 was a key step toward that goal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan by Winfield Scott to blockade the South and control the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: In 1861, Southern leaders held back their own cotton, hoping a shortage would force Britain to help them, but one part of this plan soon made shipping cotton overseas much harder anyway. As that part tightened, prices of salt, coffee, and other goods soared across the Confederacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union strategy of Winfield Scott, which combined a naval blockade with a campaign down the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: The author of this plan, a Virginian who stayed loyal to the Union, had commanded the brigade that won the Battle of Chippawa in the War of 1812 and led the army that captured Mexico City in 1847. He retired in November 1861, and George McClellan replaced him.
tossups.r: That general was Winfield Scott. For 10 points, name his plan to defeat the Confederacy by blockading its coast and seizing the Mississippi River.

clues.t: Proposed in 1861 by Winfield Scott, the Union army’s 74-year-old general-in-chief
Part one: a naval blockade of Southern ports along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts
Part two: gunboats and troops would take control of the Mississippi River and split the Confederacy in two
Named after a giant South American snake that squeezes its prey
A Union strategy for winning the American Civil War (1861–1865)
Ulysses S. Grant’s capture of Vicksburg, Mississippi (July 4, 1863), was the key victory on the river

Lincoln then wrote that “the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea”

The _Prize Cases_ (1863): the Supreme Court upheld Lincoln’s blockade, 5–4, even without a declaration of war
Fort Fisher fell in January 1865, closing Wilmington, North Carolina, the most important port left for blockade runners

trap.title: Plan, river, or siege?
trap.body: This plan’s two halves lead to other answer lines: the Mississippi River, and battles on it like the Siege of Vicksburg. If a question asks for “this river,” “this siege,” or “this war,” naming the plan is wrong, and naming the river when it asks for “this plan” or “this strategy” is wrong too. Players also mix it up with the Marshall Plan, a different “plan” answer, or with Sherman’s “total war” March to the Sea.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this plan” or “this strategy” wants the Anaconda Plan. Winfield Scott, a blockade, a snake, or squeezing the South means the plan; Grant, John C. Pemberton, and a siege of more than six weeks mean Vicksburg. If you just say “the blockade,” expect a prompt, so add the plan’s name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Anaconda Plan (prompt on the Union blockade of the South, Scott’s plan, or Scott’s Great Snake)

topics.name: Anne Hutchinson
topics.kicker: Puritan dissenter banished from Massachusetts Bay · Co-founded Portsmouth, R.I.
topics.briefing: In the 1630s, Anne Hutchinson, a midwife and mother of 15, packed her Boston home with neighbors eager to hear her discuss the week’s sermons, and she told them that most of the colony’s ministers were teaching salvation the wrong way. In 1637, Massachusetts Bay’s leaders put her on trial, and Governor John Winthrop’s court banished her as “a woman not fit for our society.” She helped found Portsmouth, in what became Rhode Island.
topics.answerHtml: Anne Hutchinson (or Anne Marbury; do not accept “Thomas Hutchinson”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the first chapter of _The Scarlet Letter_, Nathaniel Hawthorne writes that a wild rosebush beside the prison door may have “sprung up under the footsteps” of this “sainted” woman as she entered the prison. Hawthorne had earlier written a short biographical sketch of this woman.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Puritan woman who was banished from Massachusetts Bay during the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: Cyrus Dallin made a 1922 statue of this woman that stands outside the Massachusetts State House. A river and a parkway in the Bronx and Westchester County, New York, are named for her because she spent her last months nearby.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who held religious meetings in her Boston home and was banished by John Winthrop’s government.

tossups.p: This woman’s father, the clergyman Francis Marbury, was jailed for criticizing how poorly the Church of England trained its ministers. She was born in Alford, Lincolnshire, and in 1634 she followed the minister John Cotton across the Atlantic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Puritan woman who was put on trial in 1637 and banished from Massachusetts Bay.

tossups.p: The young governor Henry Vane supported this woman, but he lost the 1637 election to a rival and soon went home to England. Her brother-in-law John Wheelwright was banished after giving a controversial fast-day sermon, and he went on to found Exeter, New Hampshire.
tossups.r: That rival, John Winthrop, presided over her trial. For 10 points, name this Boston woman at the center of the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: This woman taught that people are saved by a “covenant of grace,” not a “covenant of works,” and she accused most of her colony’s ministers of preaching works. Her enemies labeled her ideas with a word meaning “against the law.”
tossups.r: That word was “Antinomian.” For 10 points, name this woman who was banished from Massachusetts Bay after her 1637 trial.

tossups.p: This woman worked as a midwife and healer and had fifteen children with her husband, William, a merchant. She praised the preaching of John Cotton but said that most other ministers in her colony were preaching a “covenant of works.”
tossups.r: She held weekly meetings in her home to discuss sermons. For 10 points, name this Puritan woman at the center of the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: In 1637, a gathering of New England ministers at Newtown, later renamed Cambridge, condemned dozens of religious “errors” linked to this woman and her followers. That November, the colony’s General Court put her on trial in the same town.
tossups.r: Governor John Winthrop led that trial. For 10 points, name this Puritan woman who was banished as “a woman not fit for our society.”

tossups.p: During her trial, this woman cited the Bible’s Letter to Titus to defend teaching other women, and she answered her questioners skillfully until she said that God spoke to her through “immediate revelation.” That claim sealed her conviction.
tossups.r: Governor John Winthrop’s court then banished her from Massachusetts Bay. For 10 points, name this Puritan dissenter.

tossups.p: In March 1638, this woman was excommunicated by the First Church of Boston, where her longtime minister, John Cotton, had turned against her. Mary Dyer, who was later hanged on Boston Common after returning to Massachusetts as a Quaker, walked out of the church beside her.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who had been banished from Massachusetts Bay during the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: This woman and her followers settled on Aquidneck [“uh-KWID-nek”] Island in 1638 after Roger Williams helped them buy land from the Narragansett. William Coddington and others had signed a compact to found the town of Portsmouth there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who moved to what became Rhode Island after being banished from Massachusetts Bay.

tossups.p: After her husband died, this woman moved to New Netherland and settled near Pelham Bay, in what is now the Bronx. In 1643, during a war between Dutch colonists and local Native peoples, she and most of the family living with her were killed, but her young daughter Susanna was taken captive and later returned.
tossups.r: Years earlier, she had helped found Portsmouth in what became Rhode Island. For 10 points, name this woman who had been banished from Massachusetts Bay after the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: Puritan critics called this woman the “American Jezebel,” a phrase Eve LaPlante later used as the title of a 2004 biography of her. A Puritan governor’s account of her trial was published in 1644 in a book about the “Rise, Reign, and Ruin” of her followers.
tossups.r: That governor was John Winthrop. For 10 points, name this woman banished during the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: This woman’s great-great-grandson Thomas became the royal governor of Massachusetts and refused to let the tea ships leave Boston Harbor in 1773. She had arrived in Boston in 1634 with her husband, William, and their many children.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose meetings to discuss sermons led to the Antinomian Controversy.

tossups.p: After this woman’s trial, the colony’s General Court ordered dozens of her supporters to hand over their guns and ammunition, fearing they might rebel. Many of those men had signed a petition defending her brother-in-law John Wheelwright.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whom John Winthrop’s court banished as “a woman not fit for our society.”

tossups.p: Some historians call the dispute centered on this woman the “Free Grace Controversy,” since she stressed God’s free gift of grace over good works. Deputy Governor Thomas Dudley was one of her sharpest questioners at her trial.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman banished from Massachusetts Bay, whose dispute with the colony’s ministers is usually called the Antinomian Controversy.

clues.t: Central figure in the Antinomian Controversy (1636–1638) in the Massachusetts Bay Colony
Held meetings in her Boston home to discuss sermons, first for women and then for men too
Tried in 1637 and banished from the colony as “a woman not fit for our society”
Governor John Winthrop presided over her trial and led the case against her
Moved to Aquidneck Island and helped found Portsmouth (1638), in what became Rhode Island
Taught a “covenant of grace” and accused most ministers of preaching a “covenant of works”
Critics called her ideas “Antinomian,” meaning “against the law”
Followed minister John Cotton to Massachusetts in 1634; he later turned against her
At her trial, she said God spoke to her through “immediate revelation,” which sealed her conviction
A midwife and healer, and the mother of 15 children with her husband, William, a merchant
Like Roger Williams, banished by Massachusetts Bay; Williams helped her group buy Aquidneck Island from the Narragansett
Excommunicated by the First Church of Boston (March 1638); Mary Dyer walked out of the church beside her
Killed with most of her household in 1643 in New Netherland, near Pelham Bay (now in the Bronx), during a war between the Dutch and local Native peoples
Supported by young governor Henry Vane and by her brother-in-law John Wheelwright, who was banished and founded Exeter, New Hampshire
Hawthorne’s _The Scarlet Letter_: a rosebush by the prison door may have sprung up under the footsteps of this “sainted” woman
Cyrus Dallin’s 1922 statue of her stands outside the Massachusetts State House
A river and a parkway in the Bronx and Westchester County, New York, are named for her
Daughter of clergyman Francis Marbury, who was jailed for criticizing poorly trained ministers; born in Alford, Lincolnshire, England
A 1637 synod of ministers at Newtown (later Cambridge) condemned dozens of “errors” tied to her group; her trial was held there too
At her trial, cited the Bible’s Letter to Titus to defend women teaching other women
Puritan critics called her the “American Jezebel”; Winthrop’s account of her trial is in _A Short Story of the Rise, Reign, and Ruin of the Antinomians_ (1644)
Her great-great-grandson Thomas was the royal governor of Massachusetts at the time of the Boston Tea Party (1773)
After her trial, dozens of supporters who had signed a petition for Wheelwright were disarmed: ordered to give up their guns
Her young daughter Susanna was taken captive in the 1643 attack and later returned
The dispute is also called the “Free Grace Controversy”; Deputy Governor Thomas Dudley questioned her sharply
William Coddington and others signed the Portsmouth Compact (1638); Coddington later founded Newport (1639)

trap.title: Which banished Puritan?
trap.body: Massachusetts Bay banished two famous dissenters in the 1630s, and both ended up in what became Rhode Island. Roger Williams was banished in 1635 and founded Providence; Anne Hutchinson was banished after her 1637 trial and helped found Portsmouth. Saying “Williams” on a Hutchinson question loses the tossup, and so does “Thomas Hutchinson,” her great-great-grandson, who was royal governor during the Boston Tea Party.
trap.fix: Hutchinson clues: a woman, a midwife, meetings in her home, the covenant of grace, the Antinomian Controversy, and John Winthrop’s trial. Williams clues: separation of church and state, the Narragansett, _The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution_, and Providence. If you hear tea ships or the Boston Massacre, the Hutchinson they want is Thomas.
trap.line: Real answer line: Anne Hutchinson (or Anne Marbury; do not accept “Thomas Hutchinson”)

topics.name: Annie Oakley
topics.kicker: Sharpshooting star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West · Nicknamed “Little Sure Shot”
topics.briefing: Annie Oakley grew up poor in rural Ohio and began hunting as a girl to help feed her family. She became the most famous sharpshooter in the world as a star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, splitting playing cards held edge-on and hitting targets behind her by aiming with a mirror. Sitting Bull nicknamed her “Little Sure Shot,” and the musical _Annie Get Your Gun_ tells a made-up version of her love story with the marksman Frank Butler.
topics.answerHtml: Annie Oakley (or Phoebe Ann Mosey; prompt on Annie, Phoebe, or Little Sure Shot)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This woman was born with the last name Mosey. She began trapping and hunting as a young girl in Darke County, Ohio, and the game she sold helped pay off the mortgage on her mother’s farm.
tossups.r: Sitting Bull later nicknamed her “Little Sure Shot.” For 10 points, name this sharpshooter who starred in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: This woman beat the traveling marksman Frank Butler in a shooting match, and the two later married. Butler eventually stopped performing his own act so that he could manage hers and serve as her assistant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Ohio-born sharpshooter, the star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, who inspired the musical _Annie Get Your Gun_.

tossups.p: In 1884, the Lakota leader Sitting Bull watched this performer in St. Paul, Minnesota, and was so impressed that he adopted her as an honorary daughter. A year later, both of them joined the same traveling show.
tossups.r: Sitting Bull nicknamed her “Little Sure Shot.” For 10 points, name this star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: Free tickets and passes were once nicknamed for this woman, because the holes punched in them looked like the bullet holes in the playing cards she shot. She could split a card held edge-on and shoot over her shoulder by aiming with a mirror.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sharpshooter nicknamed “Little Sure Shot,” the star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: In 1894, this performer showed off her shooting for a short film made at Thomas Edison’s Black Maria studio in New Jersey. At the time, she was a star of a traveling show that featured cowboys, Native American riders, and a staged attack on a stagecoach.
tossups.r: That show was Buffalo Bill’s Wild West. For 10 points, name this sharpshooter known as “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: During Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee year of 1887, this performer amazed crowds in London, including the queen herself, while touring England with an American show. She had joined that show two years earlier, and her final season with it came in 1901.
tossups.r: That show was Buffalo Bill’s Wild West. For 10 points, name this American sharpshooter nicknamed “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: A popular story says that this sharpshooter once shot the ash off a cigarette held by Wilhelm II of Germany, the ruler who later led his country into World War I. She supposedly joked afterward that if she had missed, she might have prevented that war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Ohio sharpshooter who toured Europe with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: When war with Spain seemed close in 1898, this woman wrote to President William McKinley offering to raise a company of fifty women sharpshooters. McKinley never took her up on the offer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sharpshooter nicknamed “Little Sure Shot,” who starred for years in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: After newspapers owned by William Randolph Hearst falsely reported in 1903 that this woman had been arrested for stealing, she spent years suing dozens of newspapers for libel and won most of the cases. The woman who had actually been arrested was using a stage name like hers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sharpshooter from Ohio, nicknamed “Little Sure Shot,” who starred in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: This performer left a famous traveling show after she was hurt when its train crashed into another train in North Carolina in 1901. After she recovered, she kept giving shooting exhibitions and teaching women to shoot.
tossups.r: That show was Buffalo Bill’s Wild West. For 10 points, name this sharpshooter nicknamed “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: This woman died in Greenville, Ohio, in 1926, and her husband, Frank Butler, died just eighteen days later. As a girl, she had sold the quail and rabbits she shot to a shopkeeper in Greenville.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sharpshooter who starred in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and was nicknamed “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: Ethel Merman starred as this woman in a 1946 Broadway musical whose songs include “There’s No Business Like Show Business” and “Anything You Can Do.” Irving Berlin wrote the music and lyrics for that show.
tossups.r: That musical is _Annie Get Your Gun_. For 10 points, name this real-life sharpshooter from Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: Gail Davis played this woman in a 1950s TV western. Betty Hutton played her in a 1950 movie musical, and Bernadette Peters won a Tony Award for playing her in a 1999 Broadway revival of that musical.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sharpshooter who inspired the musical _Annie Get Your Gun_.

tossups.p: This sharpshooter believed that women should learn to shoot for sport and self-defense, and over the years she taught thousands of women how to handle a gun. Her trick shots included hitting a dime tossed into the air.
tossups.r: Sitting Bull called her “Little Sure Shot.” For 10 points, name this star of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West.

tossups.p: As a young girl, this future performer was sent to work for a family that she later called “the wolves” because they treated her so harshly, and she eventually ran away from them. After she returned home, her hunting helped support her family.
tossups.r: She grew up to star in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West. For 10 points, name this Ohio sharpshooter nicknamed “Little Sure Shot.”

Sitting Bull nicknamed her “Little Sure Shot”
Inspired Irving Berlin’s 1946 musical _Annie Get Your Gun_
Grew up poor in Darke County, Ohio, and began hunting as a girl to help feed her family
Beat marksman Frank Butler in a shooting match and later married him; he became her manager
Her parents named her Phoebe Ann; her family’s last name was Mosey
Split playing cards held edge-on and shot over her shoulder by aiming with a mirror

Performed in London for Queen Victoria during her Golden Jubilee year (1887)

The game she shot and sold helped pay off the mortgage on her mother’s farm
Ethel Merman starred in that musical, whose songs include “There’s No Business Like Show Business” and “Anything You Can Do”

Filmed showing off her shooting at Thomas Edison’s Black Maria studio in New Jersey (1894)
Offered President McKinley a company of 50 women sharpshooters for the Spanish-American War (1898)
A popular story: she shot the ash off a cigarette held by Germany’s Wilhelm II and later joked that missing might have prevented World War I
Sued dozens of newspapers for libel after Hearst papers falsely reported her arrest (1903); she won most of the cases

Played by Gail Davis in a 1950s TV western, Betty Hutton in a 1950 film, and Bernadette Peters in a 1999 Broadway revival

Her trick shots included hitting a dime tossed into the air

Starred in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West for most of the sixteen years from 1885 to 1901 and toured Europe with it more than once

trap.title: Not Calamity Jane!
trap.body: Two famous women of the Wild West get mixed up. Annie Oakley was a sharpshooter from Ohio who performed in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West; Calamity Jane was a frontierswoman linked to Deadwood, in the Dakota Territory, and to Wild Bill Hickok. A question about the musical _Annie Get Your Gun_ may also ask for the show itself, and early clues about Buffalo Bill or Frank Butler can tempt you to name the wrong person.
trap.fix: Oakley clues: Ohio, Frank Butler, Sitting Bull’s nickname “Little Sure Shot,” trick shots with playing cards and mirrors, and Queen Victoria. Calamity Jane clues: Deadwood and Wild Bill Hickok. Listen for “this woman” versus “this musical,” and if you only say “Annie,” expect a prompt.

topics.name: Antonio López de Santa Anna
topics.kicker: Mexican general and president · Took the Alamo, lost Texas at San Jacinto
topics.briefing: Antonio López de Santa Anna called himself the “Napoleon of the West” and served as Mexico’s president many times between 1833 and 1855. In 1836, his army stormed the Alamo, but weeks later Sam Houston’s Texans routed him at San Jacinto in about 18 minutes and captured him the next day. He lost his left leg fighting the French in 1838, and he later had it buried with full military honors.
topics.answerHtml: Antonio López de Santa Anna (prompt on López or the Napoleon of the West)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1842, this man had his amputated leg dug up and reburied in Mexico City with full military honors, but two years later, after he fell from power, an angry crowd pulled it from its tomb and dragged it through the streets. He had lost that leg defending Veracruz against the French in 1838.
tossups.r: That conflict was the Pastry War. For 10 points, name this Mexican general who won at the Alamo but lost at San Jacinto.

tossups.p: Soldiers of the 4th Illinois Infantry captured this man’s artificial leg at the Battle of Cerro Gordo [“SAIR-oh GOR-doh”], and it has long been kept at a military museum in Springfield, Illinois. Two months earlier, he had attacked Zachary Taylor’s army at Buena Vista [“BWAY-nuh VEE-stuh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who commanded his country’s army in the Mexican-American War.

tossups.p: While a prisoner, this man signed the Treaties of Velasco [“veh-LAHS-koh”] with David Burnet, agreeing to pull his troops back beyond the Rio Grande and secretly promising to work for Texas independence. His own government refused to accept those treaties.
tossups.r: He had been captured after losing the Battle of San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this Mexican general and president.

tossups.p: The day after a battle that lasted about 18 minutes, Texian soldiers caught this man hiding in a common soldier’s clothes. Other Mexican prisoners revealed who he was by calling out “El Presidente” when he was brought into camp.
tossups.r: That battle was San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this Mexican leader whose army had won at the Alamo weeks earlier.

tossups.p: This man lost his left leg to cannon fire while fighting French troops at Veracruz in a war that began partly over damage to a French pastry cook’s shop. That wound made him a national hero again after his earlier defeat in Texas.
tossups.r: That conflict was the Pastry War. For 10 points, name this Mexican general who had besieged the Alamo in 1836.

tossups.p: In 1853, this man’s government sold the United States land south of the Gila [“HEE-luh”] River for 10 million dollars, money he badly needed to pay for his army. That deal, negotiated by the American minister James Gadsden, gave the United States a southern route for a railroad.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican leader who called himself “His Most Serene Highness” and had earlier commanded at the Alamo.

tossups.p: This man became known as the “Hero of Tampico” after he defeated a Spanish army that landed in Mexico in 1829 hoping to win it back. Years earlier, he had been an officer in the Spanish army before switching sides to support Agustín de Iturbide [“ah-goo-STEEN day ee-toor-BEE-day”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who served as president many times and lost Texas in 1836.

tossups.p: After becoming president in 1833, this man turned against the federal Constitution of 1824 and his own liberal vice president, Valentín Gómez Farías [“vah-len-TEEN GOH-mez fah-REE-us”]. In 1835, he crushed a revolt by the state of Zacatecas [“zah-kah-TAY-kus”] against his government.
tossups.r: Texans also rebelled against him. For 10 points, name this Mexican general who besieged the Alamo in 1836.

tossups.p: After his troops captured James Fannin’s men in March 1836, this general ordered that hundreds of those prisoners be executed at Goliad [“GOH-lee-ad”]. Weeks later, Texian soldiers shouted “Remember Goliad!” as they charged his army.
tossups.r: That charge came at San Jacinto, where he was defeated and captured. For 10 points, name this Mexican general who had won at the Alamo.

tossups.p: When this general’s army began its siege of an old mission in San Antonio, it raised a red flag, and during the final attack its buglers played the “Degüello” [“day-GWAY-yoh”]; both signaled that no mercy would be shown. William Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett died in that attack.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who won the Battle of the Alamo in 1836.

tossups.p: After months in captivity in Texas, this man traveled to Washington, D.C., where he met President Andrew Jackson in January 1837. Back home, Mexico’s government refused to honor the treaties he had signed while he was a prisoner.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who had been captured after losing the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836.

tossups.p: In 1846, the U.S. Navy let this exiled leader pass through its blockade from Cuba, because President James K. Polk believed he would help make peace. Instead, he took command of his country’s army and fought against the Americans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who had won at the Alamo ten years earlier.

tossups.p: Returning to power in 1853, this man ruled as a dictator and insisted on being called “His Most Serene Highness.” The Revolution of Ayutla [“ah-YOOT-lah”], led by Juan Álvarez, drove him from power for the last time in 1855.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican leader who served as president many times and sold land to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase.

tossups.p: While living in exile on Staten Island, New York, in the 1860s, this man is credited with introducing the inventor Thomas Adams to chicle, a tree gum that Adams turned into chewing gum. He later returned to Mexico under an amnesty and died poor in Mexico City in 1876.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Mexican president who lost the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836.

tossups.p: This man served as his country’s president many times between 1833 and 1855, often leaving the daily work of governing to others while he stayed at his estate near Veracruz. He liked to call himself the “Napoleon of the West.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mexican general who lost Texas at the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836.

clues.t: His army besieged and stormed the Alamo in San Antonio (February 23–March 6, 1836)
Lost to Sam Houston at San Jacinto (April 21, 1836) in about 18 minutes and was captured the next day

Led Mexico’s army against the Texas Revolution (1835–1836)
Commanded Mexico’s army in the Mexican-American War (1846–1848)

In 1846, President Polk let him pass through the U.S. blockade from exile in Cuba, hoping he would make peace
At the Alamo, his army raised a red flag when the siege began and played the “Degüello” bugle call in the final attack, both meaning no mercy
Had his amputated leg reburied with full military honors (1842); a mob dug it up after his fall from power (1844)

trap.title: Which side, which war?
trap.body: Santa Anna shows up in two wars a decade apart: the Texas Revolution (the Alamo, Goliad, and San Jacinto in 1836) and the Mexican-American War (Buena Vista and Cerro Gordo in 1847). Players who buzz early on “San Jacinto” sometimes blurt out Sam Houston, the Texian general who beat him, and questions about the Alamo or the Gadsden Purchase may want the event rather than the man.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man” or “this general,” then ask which side he was on. The Mexican leader who called himself the “Napoleon of the West,” lost a leg in the Pastry War, and served as president many times is Santa Anna. Sam Houston commanded the Texian army and became the first elected president of the Republic of Texas.
trap.line: Real answer line: Antonio López de Santa Anna (prompt on López or the Napoleon of the West)

topics.name: Atlanta
topics.kicker: Capital and largest city of Georgia · Birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr.
topics.briefing: Atlanta began in 1837 as Terminus, the spot chosen as the end of a new railroad line in the Georgia woods. It grew into the South’s great rail hub, which is why William Tecumseh Sherman’s Union army captured it and burned much of it in 1864. The city rebuilt itself, chose a phoenix rising from the ashes as its symbol, and became the birthplace of Coca-Cola and Martin Luther King Jr. and the host of the 1996 Olympics.
topics.answerHtml: Atlanta, Georgia (prompt on its earlier names, Terminus or Marthasville; do not accept “Georgia”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This city began in 1837 as Terminus, the spot chosen as the end of the Western and Atlantic Railroad, and in 1843 it was renamed Marthasville in honor of a former governor’s daughter. A stone Zero Mile Post marked the original end of that railroad line.
tossups.r: In 1845 it took its present name, based on the word “Atlantic.” For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: In September 1864, an army commander ordered civilians to leave this city and told its mayor, James Calhoun, that “war is cruelty, and you cannot refine it.” Earlier that summer, Jefferson Davis had replaced Joseph E. Johnston with John Bell Hood as the general defending this city.
tossups.r: William Tecumseh Sherman’s troops burned much of this city before the March to the Sea. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: A huge circular painting displayed at this city’s history center shows a July 1864 battle in which Union general James McPherson was killed. Visitors view that cyclorama from a platform in the middle of the room, surrounded by the scene.
tossups.r: Weeks after that battle, William Tecumseh Sherman’s army captured this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: In 1886, pharmacist John Pemberton created a soft drink in this city, and his bookkeeper, Frank Robinson, gave it its name and wrote that name in the flowing script that became its famous logo. Asa Candler, who bought the company and built it into a giant, later served as this city’s mayor.
tossups.r: That drink was Coca-Cola. For 10 points, name this Georgia city, which also hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics.

tossups.p: A national historical park in this city includes the house at 501 Auburn Avenue and Ebenezer Baptist Church, where a famous father and son both served as pastors. The son entered this city’s Morehouse College when he was only 15.
tossups.r: That son, Martin Luther King Jr., was born here in 1929. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: In 1996, security guard Richard Jewell spotted a suspicious backpack in this city’s Centennial Olympic Park and helped move people away before the bomb inside it exploded. Jewell was wrongly suspected of the crime and later cleared, a story told in a 2019 Clint Eastwood film.
tossups.r: That park was built for the 1996 Summer Olympics, where Muhammad Ali lit the cauldron at the opening ceremony. For 10 points, name this Georgia city.

tossups.p: At the Cotton States and International Exposition held in this city in 1895, Booker T. Washington told his audience to “cast down your bucket where you are.” W. E. B. Du Bois, who taught for years at a university in this city, later attacked that speech as a “compromise.”
tossups.r: That speech is often named for this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, the birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr.

tossups.p: A federal agency that grew out of a World War II office fighting malaria in the South was founded in this city in 1946 as the Communicable Disease Center. That agency, the CDC, has kept its headquarters here, next to Emory University.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, which hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics.

tossups.p: Scarlett O’Hara flees this city as it burns in Margaret Mitchell’s 1936 novel _Gone with the Wind_, and the 1939 film of that novel had its world premiere here. Hattie McDaniel, who won an Oscar for that film, could not attend the premiere because of segregation.
tossups.r: Mitchell herself lived in this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, which Union troops burned in 1864.

tossups.p: On April 8, 1974, Hank Aaron hit his 715th career home run in this city, breaking Babe Ruth’s record. As he neared that record, Aaron had received thousands of hateful letters, many of them racist.
tossups.r: His team, the Braves, had moved to this city from Milwaukee in 1966. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: Maynard Jackson became the first Black mayor of this city in 1974, and its airport is named for him and for William Hartsfield, a mayor who called it “the city too busy to hate.” That airport has often been ranked the busiest in the world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, which hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics and is the home of Coca-Cola.

tossups.p: This city’s seal shows a phoenix rising from flames above the Latin motto “Resurgens,” meaning “rising again.” In the 1880s, Henry Grady, editor of this city’s _Constitution_ newspaper, became famous for promoting an industrial “New South.”
tossups.r: The phoenix recalls how this city rebuilt after Union troops burned much of it in 1864. For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia.

tossups.p: Socialist Eugene V. Debs ran for president in 1920 from a federal prison in this city, where he was serving a sentence for a speech against World War I, and he won nearly a million votes. In 1934, Al Capone was moved from that same prison to Alcatraz.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia city, the home of Coca-Cola and the birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr.

tossups.p: Ted Turner launched CNN, the first 24-hour cable news channel, from this city in 1980, and he also owned this city’s baseball team. Delta Air Lines has long had its headquarters here, near the city’s giant airport.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, where Coca-Cola was invented in 1886.

tossups.p: The Carter Center and Jimmy Carter’s presidential library stand in this city, and the civil rights leader John Lewis represented much of it in Congress from 1987 to 2020. Andrew Young, a former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, served as its mayor in the 1980s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital of Georgia, the birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr. and the home of Coca-Cola.
